name: Clinical Decision Support Software
blurb: When decision support AI is regulated as a device.
title: Clinical Decision Support Software
answer: Whether clinical decision support software is regulated by the FDA depends on its intended use. Under the FDA's 2022 guidance, software that lets a clinician independently review the basis for a recommendation can fall outside device rules, while tools that analyse images or signals, or drive time critical decisions, are regulated devices.

reading.body:
Whether clinical decision support software is regulated as a medical device turns on intended use, not on whether it uses AI. Under the FDA's 2022 guidance, software that lets a clinician independently review the basis for a recommendation can fall outside device rules, while tools that analyse images or signals, or drive time critical decisions, are regulated devices.

The dividing line is the clinician's ability to check the reasoning. A tool that surfaces a recommendation and the evidence behind it leaves the judgement with the person. A tool that reads an image or a signal and returns a finding the clinician cannot reconstruct has taken over part of the decision, and that is what triggers device review.

For AI specifically, this matters because the same model can sit on either side of the line depending on how it is packaged and what it claims to do. Capability is not the test. Intended use is. A care team evaluating a vendor should ask whether the tool is FDA authorized or relies on the non-device CDS criteria, and what that means for the evidence behind it.

The data covers the 2022 guidance and its criteria. It does not cover how the FDA has applied those criteria in specific clearances, how state law or payer rules interact with them, or how the line has been drawn for any particular product.

sections.body: Ask vendors whether their tool is FDA authorized or relies on the non-device CDS criteria, and what that means for evidence.
